subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A medical student reviewing a skeletal radiology atlas asks about the relative frequency of bone tumors. She notes that most lytic lesions she sees are secondary deposits from carcinomas rather than tumors arising from bone itself. She also recalls that benign and malignant primary bone tumors follow different naming conventions.
question: Which of the following statements about bone tumors is correct?

options.text: Primary bone tumors are more common than metastatic bone disease
Benign bone tumors typically end in '-sarcoma'
Metastatic bone disease is more common than primary bone tumors, and benign tumors typically end in '-oma'
All primary bone tumors arise in the diaphysis of long bones
Benign bone tumors are always asymptomatic

explanation_correct: Metastatic disease involving bone is more common than any primary bone tumor. Primary benign bone tumors are generally named with the suffix '-oma' (eg, osteoma, chondroma), whereas malignant primary bone tumors usually end in '-sarcoma' (eg, osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma). This naming and frequency framework is the starting point for classifying skeletal lesions.

explanation_incorrect.A: The reverse is true: metastases from breast, lung, prostate, kidney, and thyroid carcinoma far outnumber primary bone tumors.
explanation_incorrect.B: Benign tumors end in '-oma'; the suffix '-sarcoma' denotes a malignant mesenchymal tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Primary bone tumors have characteristic sites: osteochondroma and osteosarcoma favor the metaphysis, whereas giant cell tumor and chondroblastoma arise in the epiphysis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Many benign tumors, such as osteoid osteoma, cause substantial pain, typically worse at night.

educationalObjective: Recognize that bone metastases are more common than primary bone tumors and that benign primary tumors end in '-oma' while malignant ones end in '-sarcoma'.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 19-year-old man has a painless, slowly enlarging bump near his left knee. Radiography shows a laterally projecting ossified mass arising from the metaphysis of the distal femur. The projection is continuous with the underlying marrow cavity, is covered by a cartilaginous cap, and points away from the knee joint. He has no systemic symptoms and normal serum chemistry.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Osteochondroma (exostosis)
Osteoid osteoma
Chondrosarcoma
Giant cell tumor
Osteoma

explanation_correct: Osteochondroma, or exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumor and typically occurs in males younger than 25 years. It arises from the metaphysis of long bones, most often the distal femur around the knee, and appears as a lateral bony projection continuous with the marrow space and covered by a cartilaginous cap. The lesion characteristically points away from the joint.

explanation_incorrect.B: Osteoid osteoma is a small cortical lesion smaller than 1.5 cm in younger patients that causes nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs, not a large painless projection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chondrosarcoma is malignant, occurs in adults older than 50 years, and arises in the medulla of the pelvis or proximal long bones rather than as a capped metaphyseal projection.
explanation_incorrect.D: Giant cell tumor arises in the epiphysis after skeletal maturation, most often around the knee in women aged 20-40 years, with a soap-bubble appearance.
explanation_incorrect.E: Osteoma occurs on the surface of facial bones in middle-aged adults and is associated with Gardner syndrome.

educationalObjective: Identify osteochondroma as the most common benign bone tumor, a metaphyseal outgrowth with a cartilaginous cap that points away from the joint.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 14-year-old boy has multiple painless bony outgrowths around both knees and both shoulders. His father and paternal uncle have similar lesions. Genetic testing shows a mutation in a gene encoding an enzyme involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis. He is counseled about a small but real risk of malignant transformation of one of these lesions.
question: Which of the following best describes the underlying disorder and its major neoplastic risk?

options.text: Gardner syndrome; transformation to osteosarcoma
Li-Fraumeni syndrome; transformation to Ewing sarcoma
Hereditary multiple exostoses from EXT1/EXT2 mutation; transformation to osteosarcoma
Hereditary multiple exostoses from EXT1/EXT2 mutation; rare transformation to chondrosarcoma
Neurofibromatosis type 1; transformation to chondrosarcoma

explanation_correct: Hereditary multiple exostoses is caused by germline mutations in EXT1 or EXT2, which encode enzymes required for heparan sulfate biosynthesis. It produces multiple osteochondromas, most often around the knees and shoulders, with autosomal dominant inheritance. Malignant transformation is rare but classically leads to chondrosarcoma rather than osteosarcoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gardner syndrome causes facial osteomas and intestinal polyposis, not multiple exostoses, and is not linked to EXT genes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is due to TP53 mutation and predisposes to osteosarcoma and many other cancers, not to multiple osteochondromas.
explanation_incorrect.C: EXT1/EXT2 mutations do cause hereditary multiple exostoses, but the classic malignant transformation is to chondrosarcoma, not osteosarcoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neurofibromatosis type 1 involves NF1 and neural crest tumors; it is not associated with osteochondromas or EXT genes.

educationalObjective: Associate EXT1/EXT2 mutations with hereditary multiple exostoses and a rare risk of chondrosarcoma transformation.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 21-year-old man has 3 months of increasing pain in his right tibia. The pain is worse at night and is distinctly relieved by ibuprofen. Radiography shows a small radiolucent nidus smaller than 1.5 cm surrounded by reactive bone in the cortex of the tibia. There is no fever, weight loss, or elevated alkaline phosphatase.
question: Which of the following best explains the nocturnal pain and its response to NSAIDs?

options.text: The tumor is a giant cell tumor that produces abundant RANKL
The tumor secretes prostaglandins, which mediate the pain and are inhibited by NSAIDs
The lesion is an osteosarcoma with periosteal elevation
The tumor is an osteoblastoma that is highly sensitive to cyclooxygenase inhibition
The pain results from a pathologic fracture through a chondrosarcoma

explanation_correct: Osteoid osteoma is a small benign cortical tumor of long bones in patients younger than 25 years, with a male predominance. It produces prostaglandins, which cause characteristic bone pain that is worse at night and relieved by NSAIDs. The lesion appears as a bony mass smaller than 1.5 cm with a radiolucent osteoid nidus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Giant cell tumor occurs in the epiphysis of mature bones in adults aged 20-40 years and does not produce prostaglandin-mediated night pain.
explanation_incorrect.C: Osteosarcoma is malignant, arises in the metaphysis, and produces osteoid with a Codman triangle or sunburst pattern; NSAIDs do not relieve its pain.
explanation_incorrect.D: Osteoblastoma is histologically similar but larger than 2 cm, favors the vertebrae, and its pain is typically unresponsive to NSAIDs.
explanation_incorrect.E: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant lesion of older adults in the pelvis and proximal long bones, not a small cortical nidus.

educationalObjective: Relate osteoid osteoma's prostaglandin production to night pain relieved by NSAIDs and identify its small radiolucent nidus.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 27-year-old man has several months of persistent back pain that is not relieved by high-dose naproxen. Imaging reveals a 3 cm lytic lesion in a lumbar vertebral body with features similar to an aneurysmal bone cyst. Histology shows benign osteoid-producing osteoblasts resembling those of a smaller, NSAID-sensitive cortical tumor.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Osteoid osteoma
Osteochondroma
Chondroblastoma
Aneurysmal bone cyst
Osteoblastoma

explanation_correct: Osteoblastoma is a benign osteoid-producing tumor that favors the vertebrae and occurs more often in males. It is histologically similar to osteoid osteoma but is larger than 2 cm and causes pain that is not relieved by NSAIDs. Its radiographic appearance can mimic an aneurysmal bone cyst.

explanation_incorrect.A: Osteoid osteoma is smaller than 1.5 cm, arises in the cortex of long bones, and produces night pain that is relieved by NSAIDs.
explanation_incorrect.B: Osteochondroma is a metaphyseal outgrowth with a cartilaginous cap that points away from the joint, typically around the knee in younger patients.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chondroblastoma arises in the epiphysis before skeletal maturation in adolescents and may present with joint pain.
explanation_incorrect.D: Although the radiograph can resemble an aneurysmal bone cyst, the histology of benign osteoid-producing osteoblasts identifies an osteoblastoma.

educationalObjective: Distinguish osteoblastoma from osteoid osteoma by size, vertebral location, and lack of NSAID relief.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 32-year-old woman has progressive pain and swelling around her right knee for 6 months. Radiography shows a lytic, expansile epiphyseal lesion with a soap-bubble appearance whose epicenter is near the metaphysis. Biopsy shows neoplastic mononuclear cells expressing RANKL intermixed with reactive multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells. Her physes are closed.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this lesion?

options.text: A benign metaphyseal lesion in a boy younger than 25 years with a cartilaginous cap
A malignant small blue cell tumor of the diaphysis with t(11;22)
A locally aggressive benign epiphyseal tumor with RANKL-positive mononuclear cells and osteoclast-like giant cells
A small cortical tumor that causes NSAID-sensitive night pain
A benign epiphyseal lesion of adolescence that crosses the physis

explanation_correct: Giant cell tumor, also called osteoclastoma, occurs in adults aged 20-40 years with a female predominance and arises in the epiphysis of long bones after skeletal maturation, often around the knee. It is a locally aggressive benign tumor composed of neoplastic mononuclear cells that express RANKL plus reactive multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells. The classic soap-bubble radiographic appearance reflects its epiphyseal location with a metaphyseal epicenter.

explanation_incorrect.A: That describes osteochondroma, a metaphyseal projection with a cartilaginous cap in males younger than 25 years.
explanation_incorrect.B: That describes Ewing sarcoma, a malignant small blue cell tumor of the diaphysis with t(11;22) and onion-skin periosteal reaction.
explanation_incorrect.D: That describes osteoid osteoma, a small cortical lesion with prostaglandin-mediated night pain relieved by NSAIDs.
explanation_incorrect.E: That describes chondroblastoma, which arises in the epiphysis before skeletal maturation in adolescents and can cross the physis.

educationalObjective: Recognize giant cell tumor as a locally aggressive epiphyseal lesion after skeletal maturation with RANKL-positive mononuclear and osteoclast-like giant cells.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Pathology: Benign primary bone tumors

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 15-year-old boy has several months of pain in his left knee, worse with activity. Radiography shows a lytic lesion in the epiphysis of the distal femur that extends across the physis. He has not yet reached skeletal maturity. A similar lesion in an older adult with closed physes would more likely be a different entity.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Giant cell tumor
Chondroblastoma
Osteoid osteoma
Osteosarcoma
Osteochondroma

explanation_correct: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor of adolescents with a male predominance that arises in the epiphysis of long bones before skeletal maturation, often around the knee. It may present with joint pain and can cross the physis on radiography. In contrast, giant cell tumor arises in the epiphysis only after skeletal maturation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Giant cell tumor occurs in adults aged 20-40 years after skeletal maturation, with a soap-bubble appearance and RANKL-positive mononuclear cells.
explanation_incorrect.C: Osteoid osteoma is a small cortical lesion in long bones with night pain relieved by NSAIDs, not an epiphyseal lesion crossing the physis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Osteosarcoma is a malignant metaphyseal tumor producing osteoid, with Codman triangle or sunburst periosteal reaction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Osteochondroma is a metaphyseal outgrowth with a cartilaginous cap pointing away from the joint, not a lytic epiphyseal lesion.

educationalObjective: Differentiate chondroblastoma (epiphysis before skeletal maturation, may cross the physis) from giant cell tumor (epiphysis after maturation).
